proposals.title: Should members of Congress be subject to term limits?
proposals.description: Representatives and senators can currently serve unlimited terms, and some members have held office for over 40 years. Supporters say term limits bring fresh perspectives and reduce entrenchment; opponents say they discard experience and empower unelected staff and lobbyists.

proposals.title: Should members of Congress be banned from trading individual stocks?
proposals.description: Members of Congress may currently buy and sell individual stocks while holding office, disclosing trades after the fact. Supporters of a ban say access to non-public information makes this a conflict of interest; opponents say disclosure rules are sufficient.

proposals.title: Should Supreme Court justices serve fixed 18-year terms instead of life tenure?
proposals.description: Justices currently serve for life, and appointments depend heavily on when vacancies happen to occur. A fixed-term system would give each president a predictable number of appointments; critics say it could weaken judicial independence.

proposals.title: Should the president be elected by national popular vote instead of the Electoral College?
proposals.description: Twice in the last 25 years the presidency was won by a candidate who lost the nationwide popular vote. Supporters say every vote should count equally regardless of state; opponents say the Electoral College protects smaller states' influence.

proposals.title: Should there be a maximum age limit for serving in federal elected office?
proposals.description: There are minimum ages for federal office but no maximums. Supporters of an upper limit point to concerns about serving into advanced age; opponents say voters, not a rule, should decide who is fit to serve.

proposals.title: Should former members of Congress be banned from lobbying for five years after leaving office?
proposals.description: Current law imposes short cooling-off periods — one year for House members, two for senators — before they can lobby their former colleagues. Supporters of a longer ban say the revolving door distorts lawmaking; opponents say it limits career freedom and expertise.

proposals.title: Should congressional districts be drawn by independent commissions instead of state legislatures?
proposals.description: In most states, the party controlling the legislature draws the electoral map, and both parties have drawn districts to favor themselves. Independent commissions aim to make districts competitive; critics question whether any commission is truly neutral.

proposals.title: Should the United States adopt a national referendum process for major policy questions?
proposals.description: Unlike many democracies, the U.S. has no mechanism for citizens to vote directly on federal policy. Supporters say direct votes on major questions would increase legitimacy; opponents say complex policy is better handled through representatives.

proposals.title: Should Washington, D.C. become a state?
proposals.description: The District's roughly 700,000 residents pay federal taxes but have no voting representation in Congress. Supporters call this taxation without representation; opponents say the capital was deliberately designed not to be a state.

proposals.title: Should voters be required to show photo identification in federal elections?
proposals.description: State ID requirements currently vary widely. Supporters say uniform photo ID protects election integrity; opponents say documented in-person fraud is extremely rare and ID requirements can disenfranchise eligible voters.

proposals.title: Should every eligible citizen be automatically registered to vote?
proposals.description: In most states, citizens must register themselves before they can vote. Automatic registration through DMV and government records would add tens of millions to the rolls; critics raise concerns about roll accuracy and states' administrative burden.

proposals.title: Should the United States stop changing clocks and adopt permanent standard time?
proposals.description: Americans change clocks twice a year, a practice linked in studies to sleep disruption and a brief rise in accidents. The Senate has previously voted to end it, but no law has passed. The question splits between permanent daylight time, permanent standard time, and keeping the switch.

proposals.title: Should the federal minimum wage be raised and indexed to inflation?
proposals.description: The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 per hour since 2009, the longest freeze since it was created, though many states set higher rates. Supporters say indexing would end repeated political fights; opponents say increases cost jobs in low-margin industries.

proposals.title: Should income above the current cap (~$176,000) be subject to Social Security payroll tax?
proposals.description: Earnings above the annual cap are not taxed for Social Security, and the program's trust fund is projected to be depleted within the next decade. Lifting the cap would extend solvency; opponents call it a large tax increase that breaks the link between contributions and benefits.

proposals.title: Should the federal government be required to balance its budget except in emergencies?
proposals.description: The national debt exceeds $35 trillion and the government has run deficits in nearly every year for decades. A balanced-budget rule would force spending discipline; economists warn it could deepen recessions by forcing cuts at the worst time.

proposals.title: Should Medicare be allowed to negotiate the price of every prescription drug?
proposals.description: Medicare can currently negotiate prices for only a small list of drugs. Expanding negotiation to all drugs would lower costs for seniors and taxpayers; the pharmaceutical industry says it would reduce funding for new drug development.

proposals.title: Should background checks be required for every firearm purchase, including private sales?
proposals.description: Federal law requires background checks by licensed dealers, but private and some gun-show sales are exempt in many states. Supporters say universal checks close a gap; opponents say they burden lawful owners without stopping criminals.

proposals.title: Should cannabis be legalized at the federal level?
proposals.description: Cannabis remains federally illegal even though most states have legalized medical or recreational use, leaving banking, taxation, and enforcement in conflict. Supporters say federal law should match state reality; opponents cite health and safety concerns.

proposals.title: Should immigrants brought to the U.S. as children be given a path to citizenship?
proposals.description: Roughly two million people brought to the country as minors have grown up in legal limbo as court rulings have left the DACA program uncertain. Supporters say they are Americans in every practical sense; opponents say any legalization rewards unlawful entry.

proposals.title: Should the United States build new nuclear power plants to meet electricity demand?
proposals.description: Electricity demand is rising sharply, driven partly by data centers, and nuclear power generates carbon-free electricity around the clock. Supporters call it essential for a reliable clean grid; opponents cite cost overruns and unresolved waste storage.

proposals.title: Should AI-generated content in political advertising be required to carry a disclosure label?
proposals.description: AI tools can now produce realistic fake audio and video of candidates saying things they never said. Supporters say voters deserve to know what is synthetic; opponents raise enforcement and free-speech questions.

proposals.title: Should social media platforms be required to verify users are 16 or older?
proposals.description: Several states have passed age-verification laws now facing court challenges, and platforms' minimum ages are largely unenforced. Supporters cite evidence of harm to adolescent mental health; opponents say verification threatens everyone's privacy and anonymity.

proposals.title: Should companies be required to get opt-in consent before selling personal data?
proposals.description: The U.S. has no comprehensive federal privacy law; data brokers may buy and sell personal information largely without consent. Opt-in consent would give individuals control; industry groups say it would break ad-supported business models.

proposals.title: Should manufacturers be required to let owners repair their own devices?
proposals.description: Many manufacturers restrict access to parts, tools, and manuals, forcing repairs through authorized channels. Right-to-repair laws would guarantee owner access; manufacturers cite safety and intellectual property concerns.

proposals.title: Should the federal government invest in a national high-speed rail network?
proposals.description: The U.S. has almost no high-speed rail while peer countries operate extensive networks; projects like California's have struggled with cost and delays even as new private lines break ground. Supporters say rail cuts congestion and emissions; opponents say the record shows the money is better spent elsewhere.

proposals.title: Should Nevada restrict decorative grass statewide to conserve Colorado River water?
proposals.description: Southern Nevada already requires removal of nonfunctional turf as Lake Mead's levels remain historically low. Extending restrictions statewide would save more water; opponents say communities outside the Colorado River basin shouldn't face the same rules.

proposals.title: Should Nevada negotiate with the federal government over Yucca Mountain in exchange for benefits?
proposals.description: Congress designated Yucca Mountain as the nation's nuclear waste repository in 1987, and Nevada has fought it ever since. Some argue the state should negotiate for major federal benefits since the pressure never disappears; others say any negotiation legitimizes a project Nevadans never consented to.

proposals.title: Should public money be used to help fund professional sports stadiums?
proposals.description: Nevada approved up to $380 million in public financing for the Las Vegas baseball stadium, following earlier support for the football stadium. Supporters say pro sports drive tourism and jobs; independent economists consistently find stadium subsidies rarely pay for themselves.

proposals.title: Should Nevada dramatically expand film tax credits to attract studios?
proposals.description: Lawmakers have repeatedly debated expanding the state's modest film incentive program more than tenfold to anchor major studio campuses in Las Vegas. Supporters say it would diversify the economy beyond gaming; opponents say film credits consistently return less than they cost.

proposals.title: Should Nevada limit purchases of single-family homes by large investment firms?
proposals.description: Institutional investors have bought a significant share of homes in the Las Vegas valley, and Nevada's home prices have risen far faster than incomes. Supporters say limits would return homes to families; opponents say restricting buyers won't fix a supply shortage.

proposals.title: Should Nevada cap annual rent increases for tenants aged 62 and older?
proposals.description: Nevada currently has no limits on rent increases, and proposals to cap them for seniors on fixed incomes have failed in the legislature. Supporters say seniors are being priced out of homes they've rented for years; opponents say caps discourage the construction the state needs.

proposals.title: Should Nevada expand school-choice scholarships funded by the state?
proposals.description: Nevada's Opportunity Scholarship program lets some students attend private schools with state-supported funding, and expanding it has been among the most contested questions in the legislature. Supporters say families deserve options; opponents say it drains money from public schools.

proposals.title: Should Nevada raise the gaming tax to increase public school funding?
proposals.description: Nevada's top gaming tax rate of 6.75% is among the lowest of any state with casino gaming, while its per-pupil school funding ranks near the bottom nationally. Supporters say the industry can contribute more; opponents say raising it risks the state's competitive advantage.

proposals.title: Should Nevada amend its constitution to allow a state lottery?
proposals.description: Nevada's constitution has banned lotteries since statehood, making it one of only five states without one — and Nevadans routinely cross into California and Arizona to buy tickets. Supporters say lottery revenue should stay in the state; the gaming industry has historically opposed the competition.

proposals.title: Should Nevada restore stronger credits for rooftop solar customers?
proposals.description: Nevada cut rooftop solar credits in 2015, driving installers out of the state, then partially restored them in 2017. One of the sunniest states in the country still credits solar customers below the full retail rate; supporters want full restoration, while utilities argue solar customers shift grid costs onto everyone else.

proposals.title: Should senators be elected instead of appointed?
proposals.description: Canada's Senate reviews and can amend every law, but its members are appointed by the prime minister and serve to age 75. Supporters of election say an unelected chamber lacks legitimacy; opponents say an elected Senate would duplicate the Commons and cause gridlock.

proposals.title: Should Canada adopt proportional representation for federal elections?
proposals.description: Under first-past-the-post, a party can win a majority of seats with under 40% of the vote, and votes for losing candidates elect no one. Proportional systems match seats to vote share; critics say they produce unstable coalitions and weaken local representation.

proposals.title: Should the federal voting age be lowered to 16?
proposals.description: Sixteen-year-olds can work, pay taxes and drive in most provinces, and several democracies already let them vote. Supporters say it builds lifelong voting habits; opponents question whether the age of political maturity should move.

proposals.title: Should voting in federal elections be mandatory?
proposals.description: Australia has required voting for a century and turnout exceeds 90%, while Canadian federal turnout hovers in the 60s. Supporters say democracy is stronger when everyone participates; opponents say the right to vote includes the right not to.

proposals.title: Should federal election day be a statutory holiday?
proposals.description: Elections are held on workdays, and turnout is lowest among workers with the least schedule flexibility. A holiday would remove one barrier to voting; opponents note advance polls already run for days and question the cost.

proposals.title: Should Canada end its formal ties to the monarchy?
proposals.description: Canada's head of state is the British monarch, represented by the Governor General. Supporters of change say a sovereign country should have a Canadian head of state; opponents note the change would require unanimous provincial consent and see the monarchy as stable tradition.

proposals.title: Should interprovincial trade barriers be eliminated?
proposals.description: It is often easier to sell Canadian goods to the United States than to the next province — differing rules cover trucking, alcohol, professional licensing and more, at an estimated cost of tens of billions per year. Removing them requires provinces to give up local control they've defended for decades.

proposals.title: Should Canada phase out supply management for dairy, eggs and poultry?
proposals.description: Supply management sets production quotas and import tariffs, keeping prices stable but higher than in most countries, and it is a recurring flashpoint in trade negotiations. Supporters say it protects family farms; opponents say every household pays hundreds more per year for groceries.

proposals.title: Should foreign telecom companies be allowed to compete in Canada?
proposals.description: Canadians pay some of the highest wireless prices in the developed world, with three carriers holding most of the market. Opening the market could cut bills; opponents warn about network investment and security of critical infrastructure.

proposals.title: Should Canada actively recruit foreign grocery chains to increase competition?
proposals.description: A handful of companies control most of Canada's grocery market, and food price inflation has outpaced wages for years. Supporters say new entrants would discipline prices; skeptics note foreign chains have tried and failed to crack the market before.

proposals.title: Should Canada expand liquefied natural gas exports?
proposals.description: Canada has vast gas reserves and new export terminals are beginning to ship to Asia. Supporters say LNG creates jobs and can displace coal abroad; opponents say new fossil fuel infrastructure locks in decades of emissions.

proposals.title: Should Canada implement open banking?
proposals.description: Open banking would let you securely share your financial data with any licensed app or lender, making it easier to switch banks and compare rates. Canada has studied it for years while other countries went ahead; banks urge caution on privacy and fraud.

proposals.title: Should a new oil pipeline to tidewater be built?
proposals.description: Most Canadian oil exports flow to a single customer — the United States — at a discount. A new pipeline to the coast would open world markets; opponents cite climate commitments, Indigenous consent, and the risk of building for demand that may decline.

proposals.title: Should Canada make a major investment in Arctic infrastructure and defence?
proposals.description: Melting ice is opening Arctic shipping lanes and resource claims, and other powers are expanding their northern presence. Supporters say sovereignty must be backed by ports, roads, and forces; opponents question the cost against southern priorities.

proposals.title: Should immigration levels be tied to housing and healthcare capacity?
proposals.description: Canada's population has grown at the fastest pace in decades while housing starts and physician numbers have not kept up. Supporters say growth should match capacity; opponents say immigrants are wrongly blamed for shortages governments failed to fix.

proposals.title: Should caps on international student admissions be permanent?
proposals.description: Temporary federal caps cut international student permits sharply after years of rapid growth strained housing in college towns. Making them permanent would force institutions off tuition dependence; universities say the revenue loss guts programs Canadian students rely on.

proposals.title: Should private clinics be allowed to deliver more publicly funded surgeries?
proposals.description: Several provinces now pay private clinics to perform publicly insured operations to cut waitlists. Supporters say patients care about the wait, not the building; opponents say private delivery drains staff from hospitals and opens the door to two-tier care.

proposals.title: Should every Canadian be guaranteed access to a family doctor?
proposals.description: Millions of Canadians have no family physician and rely on walk-ins and emergency rooms. A guarantee would force provinces to train, recruit and retain primary-care providers at scale; skeptics ask what the guarantee means if the doctors don't exist.

proposals.title: Should medical assistance in dying be available for mental illness alone?
proposals.description: Parliament has repeatedly delayed extending MAID eligibility to people whose sole condition is mental illness. Supporters say excluding mental suffering is discrimination; opponents say recovery is unpredictable and safeguards are not ready.

proposals.title: Should possession of small amounts of drugs be decriminalized nationally?
proposals.description: British Columbia's decriminalization pilot was rolled back after public backlash, while overdose deaths remain a leading killer of young adults. Supporters say criminal records worsen addiction; opponents say permissive policy failed visibly in public spaces.

proposals.title: Should bail be stricter for repeat violent offenders?
proposals.description: High-profile crimes by accused out on bail pushed every premier to demand federal bail reform, and changes have already tightened rules for some offences. Supporters want further restriction; civil liberties advocates note bail is a constitutional right and jails hold many people not yet convicted.

proposals.title: Should Canada meet its NATO defence spending commitments even if it requires cuts elsewhere?
proposals.description: Canada has long spent below NATO's target and allies have grown publicly impatient. Meeting the commitment means tens of billions annually; supporters say alliance credibility depends on it, opponents say healthcare and housing need the money more.

proposals.title: Should Canada regulate advanced artificial intelligence before it is widely deployed?
proposals.description: Canada's proposed AI law died when Parliament was prorogued, leaving no binding federal rules. Supporters say safeguards must precede harm; opponents say premature rules push AI investment to other countries.

proposals.title: Should adult websites be required to verify users' ages?
proposals.description: Parliament has debated requiring age verification for sites hosting explicit content, as several countries and US states have done. Supporters say children's exposure is a public health issue; opponents say verification systems endanger every adult's privacy.

proposals.title: Should manufacturers be required to support repair of their devices in Canada?
proposals.description: Parliament amended copyright law to permit breaking digital locks for repair, but there is still no requirement that parts, tools or manuals be available. Supporters say owners should control what they own; manufacturers cite safety and design integrity.

proposals.title: Should industrial carbon pricing be maintained?
proposals.description: The consumer carbon tax is gone, but large industrial emitters still pay a price on carbon in most of the country. Supporters call it the cheapest way to cut emissions where they're largest; opponents say it burdens Canadian industry against competitors who pay nothing.

proposals.title: Should the ban on single-use plastics be maintained and expanded?
proposals.description: The federal ban on plastic bags, straws and takeout containers survived court challenges and reshaped retail. Supporters want it extended to more products; opponents say substitutes are costlier and not clearly better for the environment.

proposals.title: Should the federal government directly build public housing at scale?
proposals.description: Ottawa largely exited social housing construction in the 1990s, and advocates argue the market alone has never housed low-income Canadians. Direct building would add non-market supply; critics say governments build slowly and expensively compared to the private sector.

proposals.title: Should corporations be banned from buying single-family homes?
proposals.description: Investors own a meaningful share of Canadian housing stock, and large firms have been buying single-family homes as rental assets. Supporters say families shouldn't bid against funds; opponents say investors supply rental stock the market needs.

proposals.title: Should the CBC continue to receive public funding?
proposals.description: The CBC receives over a billion dollars annually and its role is a perennial political question. Supporters say public broadcasting binds a vast country and serves regions markets ignore; opponents say it competes unfairly with private media and should stand on its own.

proposals.title: Was returning fluoride to Calgary's drinking water the right decision?
proposals.description: Calgarians voted 62% in a 2021 plebiscite to restore fluoridation, and it returned to the water supply in 2025 — the fifth time the city has reversed itself on the question since the 1950s. Supporters cite dental health evidence; opponents object to medicating a public utility.

proposals.title: Should Calgary consider bidding for a future Winter Olympics?
proposals.description: Calgarians voted against bidding for the 2026 Games in the 2018 plebiscite, largely over cost. Supporters of a future bid say the 1988 legacy venues still give Calgary an edge; opponents say the IOC's economics haven't changed.

proposals.title: Should major city projects over $1 billion require a public vote?
proposals.description: Calgary's biggest commitments — arenas, rail lines, event centres — are decided by council alone, and the 2018 Olympic plebiscite is the rare case where citizens voted directly. Supporters say megaprojects need a mandate; opponents say referendums slow essential infrastructure.

proposals.title: Should Calgary reduce the size of city council?
proposals.description: Calgary has 14 councillors plus the mayor, each representing roughly 100,000 people. Supporters of a smaller council say it would cut cost and sharpen accountability; opponents say fewer councillors means less responsive representation as the city grows.

proposals.title: Should the CTrain be extended to the airport?
proposals.description: Calgary's airport is among the busiest in the country with no rail connection, and an airport leg has been studied for decades. Supporters say every major city connects its airport by rail; opponents point to the cost against other transit priorities.

proposals.title: Should Calgary Transit be free for riders under 18?
proposals.description: Several cities have made youth transit free to build lifelong ridership and help lower-income families. Supporters say the fare revenue lost is small against the benefit; opponents say the system needs every fare dollar for service and safety.

proposals.title: Should residential speed limits drop from 40 to 30 km/h?
proposals.description: Calgary lowered unposted residential limits to 40 km/h in 2021, and safety advocates want 30, citing collision survival rates. Opponents say 30 is impractically slow and enforcement-heavy for wide suburban streets.

proposals.title: Should Calgary fund more peace officers on transit?
proposals.description: Safety concerns on the CTrain have shaped ridership since the pandemic, and the city has repeatedly added transit officers and outreach teams. Supporters want a permanently larger presence; others say the money should fund housing and mental-health responses instead.

proposals.title: Should supervised drug consumption services operate in Calgary?
proposals.description: The Sheldon Chumir site made Calgary a flashpoint in Alberta's shift toward a recovery-focused drug strategy. Supporters say supervised sites prevent fatal overdoses; opponents cite neighbourhood disorder and favour treatment beds.

proposals.title: Should Calgary allow tiny-home villages on city land for the homeless?
proposals.description: Purpose-built villages of small homes with support services have housed people in other cities at lower cost than shelters. Supporters say city land makes them fast to build; opponents raise concerns about siting and whether they divert from permanent housing.

proposals.title: Should Calgary cap whole-home short-term rentals?
proposals.description: Thousands of Calgary homes are listed on short-term rental platforms, and the city has tightened licensing as rents climbed. Supporters of a cap say homes should house Calgarians first; opponents say hosts' property rights and tourism revenue matter too.

proposals.title: Should Calgary pause approving new suburban communities?
proposals.description: Calgary regularly approves new edge communities while committing to densification, and servicing new suburbs costs the city up front. Supporters of a pause say growth should fill the city in; opponents say restricting greenfield supply raises prices everywhere.

proposals.title: Should downtown office-to-residential conversions continue to receive city funding?
proposals.description: Calgary's conversion program is among the most ambitious in North America, turning empty towers into housing after downtown vacancy peaked near 30%. Supporters say it revives the core and the tax base; opponents question subsidizing private developers.

proposals.title: Should Calgary accelerate water main replacement even if utility rates rise?
proposals.description: The 2024 Bearspaw feeder main failure put the city under outdoor water restrictions for weeks and exposed the age of critical pipes. Faster replacement means higher water bills sooner; waiting risks another failure.

proposals.title: Should outdoor watering schedules be permanent in Calgary?
proposals.description: Calgarians lived under staged watering restrictions during the 2024 main break and drought years. A permanent schedule would lock in conservation; opponents say temporary emergencies shouldn't become permanent rules.

proposals.title: Should Calgary expand the downtown bike lane network?
proposals.description: The downtown cycle track grid has been in place for a decade, and expansion debates recur every budget cycle. Supporters say protected lanes are cheap capacity and safer streets; opponents say they take road space and parking from a car-dependent city.

proposals.title: Should residential street snow clearing be fully funded?
proposals.description: Calgary plows priority routes but residential streets largely rely on sun and traffic, and major snowfalls strand side streets for days. Full residential clearing would cost tens of millions per year; supporters call it a basic service, opponents call it a luxury in a chinook city.

proposals.title: Should Calgary Public Library expand evening and weekend hours?
proposals.description: Calgary's library system is one of the most used in North America, and branch hours were reduced in past budget rounds. Supporters say libraries are the city's most democratic space; expansion competes with every other service for budget.

proposals.title: Should the Calgary Police Service budget be increased?
proposals.description: Police funding is Calgary's single largest operating expense, and council debates it every cycle amid competing calls for more officers and for alternative crisis response. Supporters cite response times and downtown safety; opponents say new money should fund prevention.

proposals.title: Should Calgary open more off-leash dog parks?
proposals.description: Calgary has more than 150 off-leash areas, among the most anywhere, but access varies widely by neighbourhood and several have closed during construction. Supporters say demand keeps growing with density; opponents want the space protected for other park uses.
